report.source_text: After the diagnosis was confirmed, the patient received penicillin G 4 million International units (IU) intravenously six times per day for 14 days according to current guidelines.8 9 After an initial 4 days of inpatient intravenous therapy the patient was switched to an outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy via an antibiotic pump with pencillin G 24 million IU per day for the remaining days of the 14-day regimen. To additionally account for a possible need of a longer duration of treatment in later stages of infection (such as for late latent syphilis), one shot of long-acting Benzathine-Penicillin 2.4 million IU intramuscularly was added after the intravenous therapy.

report.source_text: 6 months after treatment, the patient did not notice any significant clinical amelioration. Visual acuity was still <20/200 on the right side and 20/100 on the left side. Also the ataxia had not changed. We were, however, able to demonstrate an improvement of the laboratory markers. In cerebrospinal fluid, mononuclear pleocytosis decreased from 93 to 12 cells/µL, protein levels decreased from 1.65 to 0.79 g/L and albumin decreased from 0.89 to 0.43 g/L. Furthermore, serological activity also decreased to a Treponema RPR of 1:2 after 9 months, which fulfils most current guidelines’ criteria for an adequate response to treatment (table 2).

clinician.trajectory_summary: The patient, a man in his 60s, initially presented with diplopia for 3 months, which was initially attributed to a presumed congenital IVth cranial nerve paresis. Approximately 4 years after the onset of initial symptoms, he was referred with severe neurological manifestations including gait ataxia due to diminished proprioception, absent deep tendon reflexes, Argyll-Robertson pupils, and almost complete loss of vision. A laboratory screening revealed positive syphilis serology (positive screening test, T. pallidum haemagglutination assay, RPR 1:8). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis confirmed neurosyphilis with pleocytosis (93 cells/µL), elevated protein, albumin, lactate, and intrathecal IgG synthesis against T. pallidum. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of tabes dorsalis was established. The patient was treated with a 14-day course of intravenous penicillin G, followed by intramuscular Benzathine-Penicillin. Six months post-treatment, clinical symptoms showed no significant amelioration, but CSF and serological markers demonstrated improvement.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with diplopia for 3 months.
Orthoptic diagnostics showed presumed congenital paresis of left IVth cranial nerve, exophoria, hyperopia, astigmatism, and presbyopia.
Syphilis screening test was positive, confirmed by positive T. pallidum haemagglutination assay and RPR of 1:8.
CSF study revealed pleocytosis (93 cells/µL, predominantly mononuclear), elevated protein, albumin, lactate, and intrathecal synthesis of IgG-directed against T. pallidum.

On referral (4 years after first symptoms), patient suffered from severe gait ataxia due to diminished proprioception, absent deep tendon reflexes, diminished pupillary reflex to light with preserved constriction during convergence (Argyll-Robertson pupil), and almost complete loss of vision.
Patient received penicillin G intravenously for 14 days, followed by Benzathine-Penicillin intramuscularly.
6 months after treatment, no significant clinical amelioration was noted, but laboratory markers improved (CSF pleocytosis, protein, albumin decreased; RPR decreased to 1:2).

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: The definitive diagnosis of neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis) and the presence of widespread neurological signs inconsistent with an isolated congenital cranial nerve palsy effectively ruled out the initial presumed congenital paresis as the primary cause of the patient's progressive neurological symptoms.
